method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Record consent in the medical record before transfusion**, and follow hospital transfusion procedures.
claims.source_text: All blood transfusion activity must comply with the relevant hospital procedures and guidelines … All children must have consent for blood product administration recorded in the medical record prior to transfusion
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Give a transfusion only when the expected benefit is likely to outweigh the potential hazards.**
claims.source_text: A blood transfusion should only be given when the expected benefits to the child are likely to outweigh the potential hazards
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Hb under 70 g/L: red cell transfusion is often indicated.** Lower thresholds may be acceptable if there are no clinical features (tachycardia, flow murmur, lethargy, dizziness, breathlessness, cardiac failure) and specific therapy such as iron is available.
claims.source_text: Hb (g/L) Indication <70 RBC transfusion is often indicated Lower thresholds may be acceptable in children without clinical features, eg tachycardia, flow murmur, lethargy, dizziness, shortness of breath, cardiac failure and where specific therapy (eg iron) is available
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Hb 70–90 g/L: may be indicated depending on the setting** — bleeding or haemolysis, symptoms and signs of anaemia, or uncorrected congenital heart disease.
claims.source_text: Hb (g/L) Indication … 70-90 RBC transfusion may be indicated, depending on the clinical setting, eg presence of bleeding or haemolysis, clinical signs and symptoms of anaemia Uncorrected congenital heart disease
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Hb over 90 g/L: often unnecessary and may be inappropriate**, except in specific situations such as haemoglobinopathies (thalassaemia, sickle cell disease) or congenital anaemia on a chronic transfusion program.
claims.source_text: Hb (g/L) Indication … >90 RBC transfusion is often unnecessary and may be inappropriate Transfusion may be indicated at higher thresholds for specific situations: Children with haemoglobinopathies (eg thalassaemia or sickle cell disease) or congenital anaemia on a chronic transfusion program
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Volume, under 20 kg:** mL = weight (kg) × 0.5 × desired Hb rise (g/L), prescribed in mL; **maximum Hb increment 20 g/L.** Example: 10 kg child from 60 to 80 g/L = 100 mL. **Over 20 kg: 1 unit, then reassess.**
claims.source_text: In infants and children <20 kg, transfusion volumes should be calculated based on weight, desired and actual Hb prescribed in mL maximum Hb increment should be 20 g/L … mL = wt (kg) x 0.5 x Hb (g/L) rise (desired Hb – actual Hb) Eg: 10 kg child requiring Hb rise from 60 g/L to 80 g/L 10 x 0.5 x 20 = 100 mL … >20 kg: 1 unit and re-assess
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Rate: 5 mL/kg/hr**, usual maximum about 150 mL/hr; consider starting at half the prescribed rate for the first 15 minutes.
claims.source_text: 5 mL/kg/hr Consider commencing at slower rate (eg half prescribed rate) for first 15 minutes Usual maximum rate ~150 mL/hr
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Prophylactic platelets are not indicated for immune-mediated thrombocytopenia** (ITP, HIT, TTP/HUS); congenital thrombocytopenia is an individualised decision.
claims.source_text: Immune-mediated thrombocytopaenia (eg ITP, HIT, TTP/HUS) Not indicated Congenital thrombocytopenia Individualised decision making
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **No pre-procedure platelets are needed for bone marrow aspirate or trephine, or for peripheral IV insertion.**
claims.source_text: Bone marrow aspirate or trephine biopsy Not indicated Peripheral IV insertion Not indicated
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Volume: under 15 kg, 10 mL/kg (prescribed in mL); over 15 kg, 1 unit.** Rate 10–20 mL/kg/hr — faster transfusion (e.g. over 30 minutes) may cause a reaction.
claims.source_text: In infants and children <15 kg, platelets should be prescribed in mL (10 mL/kg) … Platelet transfusion volumes in child >15 kg: 1 platelet unit … 10-20 mL/kg/hr Faster transfusion rates (eg transfused over 30 minutes) may result in a transfusion reaction
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Severe bleeding = any of:** organ dysfunction within 24 hours · haemodynamic instability (HR up or BP down by more than 20% from baseline) · Hb drop over 20% in 24 hours · measurable loss ≥5 mL/kg/hr for ≥1 hour · intraspinal bleeding with neurological loss · intra-articular bleeding limiting movement · intraocular bleeding impairing vision.
claims.source_text: Severe bleeding ANY of the following criteria Bleeding leading to at least one organ dysfunction within 24 hours Bleeding leading to haemodynamic instability (HR increase >20% from baseline or BP decrease >20% from baseline) Bleeding causing Hb drop >20% within 24 hours Quantifiable bleeding ≥5 mL/kg/hr for ≥1 hour (eg chest tube, drain) Intraspinal bleeding with loss of neurological function Non-traumatic intra-articular bleeding with decreased range of movement Intraocular bleeding impairing vision
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Moderate bleeding = all of:** more than minimal but not severe · no organ dysfunction · no haemodynamic instability · Hb drop ≤20% · measurable loss ≥1 but <5 mL/kg/hr.
claims.source_text: Moderate bleeding ALL of the following criteria: More than minimal bleeding but not meeting criteria for severe bleeding Bleeding not leading to organ dysfunction Bleeding not causing haemodynamic instability Bleeding leading to a drop of Hb ≤20% Quantifiable bleeding ≥1 mL/kg/hr but <5 mL/kg/hr (eg chest tube, drain)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **FFP is appropriate for:** acute bleeding with significant coagulopathy · warfarin reversal with significant or life-threatening bleeding (with vitamin K and prothrombinex) · liver disease with significant bleeding and coagulopathy · acute DIC with bleeding · massive haemorrhage · bleeding during or after cardiac bypass · plasma exchange for TTP · factor deficiencies with no concentrate available.
claims.source_text: FFP is appropriate for: Acute bleeding in the setting of significant coagulopathy Warfarin reversal, in the presence of significant or life-threatening bleeding (eg intracranial haemorrhage) in addition to vitamin K and prothrombinex Liver disease, with clinically significant bleeding in the context of coagulopathy Acute DIC with bleeding and significant coagulopathy During massive haemorrhage During or post-cardiac bypass for the treatment of bleeding Plasma exchange for the treatment of TTP Specific factor deficiencies where a factor concentrate is not available
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **FFP is not indicated** to correct minor INR/APTT prolongation in a non-bleeding child, for minor abnormalities in liver disease without bleeding, or to reverse an INR under 2.0 for minor procedures.
claims.source_text: FFP is NOT indicated for: Correction of minor coagulation abnormalities (minor prolongation of the INR/APTT) in a non-bleeding child Liver disease when there are minor coagulation abnormalities in a non-bleeding child For reversal of an INR <2.0 in children undergoing minor procedures
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **FFP dose: 10–20 mL/kg for all children, at 10–20 mL/kg/hr.**
claims.source_text: FFP All children: 10-20 mL/kg FFP ~277 mL Paediatric (pedipak) ~67 mL 10-20 mL/kg/hr
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Cryoprecipitate when fibrinogen is under 1.5 g/L** with active bleeding, in massive haemorrhage (or hyperfibrinolysis), or bleeding during or after cardiac bypass.
claims.source_text: Cryoprecipitate is indicated for: Active bleeding and fibrinogen level <1.5 g/L During massive haemorrhage when fibrinogen level <1.5 g/L or there is hyperfibrinolysis During or post-cardiac bypass, for the treatment bleeding when the fibrinogen level <1.5 g/L or there is hyperfibrinolysis
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Cryoprecipitate when fibrinogen is under 1.0 g/L** with acquired deficiency or acute DIC and significant bleeding, or before an invasive procedure with significant bleeding risk or at a critical site (neurosurgery, eye surgery).
claims.source_text: Acquired fibrinogen deficiency or acute DIC when there is significant bleeding and the fibrinogen <1.0 g/L Prior to an invasive procedure when the fibrinogen <1.0 g/L and there is a risk of significant bleeding associated with the surgery or it is at a critical site (eg neurosurgery or eye surgery)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Not indicated** for non-bleeding children with mildly low fibrinogen, or liver disease with minor abnormalities and no active bleeding.
claims.source_text: Cryoprecipitate is NOT indicated for: Non-bleeding children with mildly reduced fibrinogen levels Liver disease when there are minor coagulation abnormalities and no active bleeding
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Cryoprecipitate dose: 5–10 mL/kg for all children, at 10–20 mL/kg/hr.**
claims.source_text: Cryoprecipitate All children: 5-10 mL/kg Cryoprecipitate (whole blood) ~36 mL (10 mL/kg) Cryoprecipitate (apheresis) ~60 mL (5 mL/kg) 10-20 mL/kg/hr
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **In a critical bleeding event, transfuse as fast as clinically indicated.** **Every transfusion must be completed within four hours** of the product leaving blood bank.
claims.source_text: The duration/rate of the transfusion must be appropriate with the child’s clinical need, eg in a critical bleeding event, transfuse as fast as clinically indicated Transfusion must be completed within four hours of the product leaving blood bank
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Maximum prescribed volume should not exceed the equivalent adult transfusion.**
claims.source_text: Maximum prescribed volume should not be greater than the volume for equivalent adult transfusions
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Irradiated products** for all immunocompromised children (including all immunology and oncology patients), preterm and low-birth-weight neonates, neonates with cardiac disease, HLA-matched products and directed donations — to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease.
claims.source_text: Irradiated blood products Should be given to all immuno-compromised children, including all immunology and oncology patients, preterm and low birth weight neonates, neonates with cardiac disease, HLA-matched products and directed blood donations to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus host disease
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **CMV-negative products only** for neonatal exchange transfusion, neonates up to 28 days post-term, pregnant women, and CMV-negative children with SCID. At RCH, leucocyte-depleted products are an acceptable alternative.
claims.source_text: CMV negative products are only indicated for neonatal exchange transfusion, transfusions to preterm and term neonates up to 28 days post-term, pregnant women and children with severe combined immunodeficiency disease (SCID) who are CMV negative … Note: Leucocyte depleted blood products are considered an acceptable alternative to CMV seronegative products at RCH
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Phenotype-matched red cells** for chronically transfused children or red cell alloantibodies; **IgA-deficient products** for IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibody; **HLA-matched platelets** for HLA-antibody refractoriness.
claims.source_text: Phenotype matched red blood cells Indicated for children who are chronically transfused or with red cell alloantibodies IgA deficient products Children with IgA deficiency who have developed an anti-IgA antibody HLA matched platelets For children with thrombocytopaenia who are refractory to random donor platelets due to HLA antibodies
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Blood product prescription' (Last updated November 2023), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Blood_product_prescription/, retrieved 2026-09-23
